title: Design and Performance of ScAlN/AlN Trapezoidal Cantilever-Based MEMS Piezoelectric Energy Harvesters

sections.heading: Design and Performance of ScAlN/AlN Trapezoidal Cantilever-Based MEMS Piezoelectric Energy Harvesters
sections.text:
Yan Liu, Bohao Hu, Yao Cai, Jie Zhou, Wenjuan Liu, Member, IEEE, Alexander Tovstopyat, Guoqiang Wu , Senior Member, IEEE, and Chengliang Sun

Abstract—In this work, we report a method to enlarge the trapezoidal cantilever-based harvester power by using the high-performance $\mathsf { S c } _ { 0 . 2 } \mathsf { A l } _ { 0 . 8 } |$ N/aluminum nitride (AlN) composite film and introducing symmetrical corners to both sides of the beam. Energy harvesters with variable beam structure and piezoelectric film are designed and evaluated by simulations and experiments. The trapezoid with corners (TWCs) cantilever is verified to improve the output power by a factor of five times when compared with the conventional trapezoidal cantilever without corners. The maximum power density of the ScAlN/AlN-based TWC cantilever harvester is about twice that of the AlN-based harvester, reaching $2 . 0 5 4 ~ \mathrm { m W } { \cdot } \mathbf { g } ^ { - 2 } { \cdot } \mathbf { c m } ^ { - 3 }$ at a frequency of $3 3 0 . 2 5 \ \mathsf { H z }$ . The optimization of piezoelectric film and structure can give an inspiration for further improving the performance of cantilever-based energy harvesters.

Index Terms— Piezoelectric energy harvester, power output, ScAlN/aluminum nitride (AlN), trapezoid with corners (TWCs).

sections.heading: I. INTRODUCTION
sections.text:
W ITH the self-power ability, the miniaturized energyharvester provides a feasible solution to supply sustainable power for integrated microsystems [1]. In particular, piezoelectric vibration energy harvesters based on a Si MEMS process are promising as power supplies due to the effective energy harvesting mechanism and easy implementation [2]. To maximize the availability and achieve a broad application of piezoelectric energy harvesters, higher output power and efficiency are desired to obtain, for example, by a combination of structural design and material optimization [3].

The most popular design is based on the classical rectangle plain cantilever structure with variations in cantilever geometry [4]. Nonetheless, alternative designs such as trapezoidal [5], triangular [6], quadrilateral [7], and arc-shaped [8] cantilevers have been explored in an attempt to achieve high and evenly distributed stress along the cantilever length. For piezoelectric film, the most commonly used are zinc oxide $_ { ( Z \mathrm { n O ) } }$ [9], lead zirconate titanate [10] (PZT) [22], polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) [7], and aluminum nitride (AlN) [11]. Piezoelectric AlN films for MEMS energy harvesting devices offer advantages such as compatibility with a standard CMOS process, low dielectric constant, good piezoelectric coefficients, and mechanical properties, such as Young’s modulus [12], [13]. To enhance the piezoelectricity of AlN, it has been reported that Sc doping of AlN thin film can increase the value of piezoelectric strain coefficient [14].

In this work, we propose a new design of trapezoid with corners (TWCs) cantilever-based energy harvester comprised of a $\mathrm { S c } _ { 0 . 2 } \mathrm { A l } _ { 0 . 8 } \mathrm { N } / \mathrm { A l N }$ composite piezoelectric film to enhance the electric response compared with the traditional AlN-based trapezoidal harvester. The introduction of corners can directly increase the stress level away from the stem of the cantilever without damaging the beam structure. The results reveal that the novel TWC-shaped harvester with ScAlN/AlN composite thin film has a positive influence on stress distribution and power improvement.

sections.heading: II. ENERGY HARVESTER DESIGN
sections.text:
Fig. 1(a) shows our proposed structure of the cantileverbased harvester of trapezoid and TWC. The motivation of the TWC design was to reduce the spring stiffness, enhance strain distribution, and increase additional strained regions over the cantilever beam. Unlike the traditional sandwich structure with a single piezoelectric thin film, this design uses a four-stacked Mo/ScAlN/AlN/Mo composite film as the sensing layer, as shown in Fig. 1(b). The energy harvesting figure of merit (FOM) determined by the piezoelectric constant $e _ { 3 1 }$ and relative dielectric constant $\varepsilon _ { \mathrm { r } }$ is used to estimate the performance of different thin films

$$
\mathrm { F O M } = \frac { e _ { 3 1 } ^ { 2 } } { \varepsilon _ { 0 } \varepsilon _ { \mathrm { r } } } .
$$

Although ScAlN film exhibits a higher $e _ { 3 1 }$ , its permittivity $\varepsilon _ { \mathrm { r } }$ also increases [15], [16], which means more dielectric loss [17]. To compensate for the high dielectric loss of ScAlN thin film, AlN film with low dielectric permittivity is deposited underneath the ScAlN. The composite film balances the advantages and disadvantages of the single ScAlN film with high piezoelectric coefficient or high dielectric loss [Fig. 1(c)].

![](images/e54f303ae5c2d3d3a62a0818d58788f93100c071aa164e694a6e0f105080f15c.jpg)  
Fig. 1. (a) Cantilever-based energy harvesters of trapezoid and TWCs. (b) Schematic cross section of the ScAlN/AlN cantilever. (c) Analysis model of the composite film.

The distribution of stress is an important factor in evaluating the performance of energy harvesters. As shown in Fig. 2(a), the maximum first principal stress distribution of the trapezoidal beam is noted to be more explicit at the fixed constant edge. In addition, the stress is mainly distributed between the fixed end and the middle of the beam and gradually decreases away from the stem of the beam. The TWC beam can be seen as a splicing of two parts. The place where the shape changes can directly increase the stress in the nearby area. In this work, the corner is designed in the middle of the beam, and then the beam is divided into trapezoid and rectangle. As shown in Fig. 2(b), large stress appears at the corners except for the sides of the fixed clamped edge, resulting in a more uniform stress distribution over the trapezoidal part. As the angle of the corner increases, the beam is divided into two trapezoidal parts [Fig. 2(c)]. The stress at the stem and corner of the beam decreases simultaneously. When the angle of the corner decreases, the distributed stress on the beam will increase, but the stress at the corner is much higher than the fixed end [Fig. 2(d)]. Since the bending stiffness at the corner of the beam is smaller than the bending stiffness at the fixed end, higher stress will make the corners more likely to break. Similarly, when the corner position moves to the free end, the distributed stress on the beam will decrease [Fig. 2(e)]. Moving the corner closer to the fixed end will greatly increase the stress at the corner [Fig. 2(f)]. Considering the stability and output characteristics of the device comprehensively, it is optimal to place the corners in the middle of the beam and form a trapezoidal and rectangular splicing structure.

![](images/5d042083193de54909e329ed0267d28bb46e6210bacc00d210b9b24b8436bc06.jpg)  
Fig. 2. First principal stress distribution along the beams under 1-g vertical acceleration for different beam shapes. (a) Pure trapezoid. (b) Corner in the middle of the beam. (c) Larger corner in the middle of the beam. (d) Smaller corner in the middle of the beam. (e) Corner on the back half of the beam. (f) Corner on the front half of the beam.

Four different samples with variable dimensions and materials are investigated. All results presented in this article are measured on devices with a cantilever beam thickness of $5 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { { m } }$ and a mass block thickness of $5 0 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { m }$ . The resonance curves of devices are presented at an acceleration level of $1 \mathrm { \textrm { g } }$ in Fig. 3. Compared with the trapezoidal structure, the reduction of the unit bending stiffness of TWC leads to a substantial decrease in frequency, and additional strained regions simultaneously increase the output charge significantly. With the introduction of ScAlN film, the decrease of elastic stiffness constant $c _ { 3 3 }$ makes the frequency slightly shift and the increase of piezoelectric coefficient $e _ { 3 1 }$ makes the charge generated increase compared with AlN-based harvester. When using a uniform ScAlN film as the piezoelectric film, the simulation results show that the increase in output charge is very small compared with the composite film. However, increasing permittivity may lead to an increasing dielectric loss. Therefore, the use of ScAlN/AlN composite film is a way to reduce the dielectric loss without sacrificing a large amount of charge output. Besides, the piezoelectric device can be regarded as a capacitor, and a larger permittivity means a larger electrostatic capacitance. Theoretically, the open-circuit voltage of ScAlN-based harvesters will decrease as the permittivity increases $\mathbf { \nabla } ^ { \prime } V _ { \mathrm { o p e n } } = ( Q / C ) = ( Q d / \varepsilon _ { 0 } \varepsilon _ { \mathrm { r } } A ) )$ , which is undesirable. The piezoelectric material parameters [15], [18], [19] in the simulation are shown in Table I.

The surface area of larger devices is about four times that of smaller devices.

sections.heading: III. FABRICATION AND MEASUREMENT
sections.text:
The piezoelectric harvesters consisting of a silicon cantilever beam ended with an attached mass are produced by standard micromachining technology based on ScAlN/AlN platform [20]–[22]. To start, a 6-in silicon-on-insulator (SOI) wafer consisted of a $5 0 0 – \mu \mathrm { m }$ -thick handle layer, $1 - \mu \mathrm { m }$ -thick buried oxide layer, and $5 0 \mathrm { - } \mu \mathrm { m }$ device layers is used. The next step is the deposition of a Mo ${ \bf \bar { 2 0 0 } n m } )$ bottom electrode with an AlN $1 0 0 \mathrm { n m } ,$ ) seed layer, followed by the patterning of the bottom electrode [Fig. 4(a)]. The AlN $( 5 0 0 ~ \mathrm { n m } )$ and ScAlN $( 5 0 0 \ \mathrm { n m } )$ films were deposited by reactive sputtering in order. The Mo $( 2 0 0 \ \mathrm { n m } )$ top electrode deposition and patterning finish the Mo/ScAlN/AlN/Mo stack [Fig. 4(b)]. Then, thin AlN films $\mathrm { 1 0 0 ~ n m ) }$ were deposited as a passive layer. The top electrode and bottom electrode were exposed by etching the vias, respectively [Fig. 4(c) and (d)]. Al electrode pads $( 1 ~ \mu \mathrm { m } )$ were formed by the lift-off process [Fig. 4(e)]. Next, the trench patterning is done, which defines the cantilever shape [Fig. 4(f)]. The etched layers include a composite piezoelectric layer (AlN/ScAlN/AlN, $1 2 0 0 \ \mathrm { n m } ,$ , Si substrate $( 5 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { m } )$ , and oxide layer $( 1 ~ \mu \mathrm { m } )$ . On the backside of the wafer, the metal Al $( 3 0 0 ~ \mathrm { n m } )$ is prepared and patterned as a hard mask for deep reactive ion etching (DRIE) [Fig. 4(g)]. Bosch process is used to release the mass block and cantilevers. For the etching process, the piezoelectric film is etched by Corial 210 ICP-RIE etch system. The etching time of ScAlN is $50 \%$ longer than that of AlN, which means that a thicker photoresist is needed. However, the edges of thick photoresist are prone to collapse, and the photoresist near the opening will gradually become thinner, resulting in a larger etched area, as shown in Fig. 4(h). The use of ScAlN/AlN composite film can reduce the etching time and avoid defects in this process, especially for some devices with relatively high process requirements, such as film bulk acoustic resonator (FBAR). Fig. 4(i) shows the SEM image of the fabricated device. However, the thickness of the thin films is thinner than the designed value due to the deviation of the fabrication process. Fig. 4(j) and $\mathrm { ( k ) }$ shows the MEMS devices realized through the manufacturing process sketched in Fig. 1. The fabricated piezoelectric harvesters were measured using a setup illustrated in Fig. 5. During electrical measurement, each harvester was excited by applying a sinusoidal vibration with acceleration on an exciter, resulting in ac electrical power. For testing, the 6-in wafer is diced into $2 2 ~ \mathrm { m m } \times 2 2 ~ \mathrm { m m }$ dies. The die and a printed circuit board (PCB) with cavity are glued and then rigidly fixed on the calibration fixture of the exciter. Because the cantilever beams are fixed on the same die, the vibration of the cantilever will be influenced by each other, especially in the case of resonance. When measuring a single device, others need to be fixed. ![](images/70f472693bc46e8e293feaa1d0ddd05ff7c5bb15044ce3e4eec690893fb6c12b.jpg) Fig. 5. Experimental setup for output measurements. The device is rigidly fixed on the exciter (B&K 4808). The amplitude and frequency can be controlled by software (B&K PULSE Labshop) and power amplifier (B&K 2719). The output charge signal is converted into a voltage signal by a conditioning amplifier (NEXUS 2692) and then read by the front-end setup (B&K 3160). sections.heading: IV. EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
sections.text:
The design objective is to maximize the power generation through coupling the load resistance experienced by the harvester. Fig. 6(a)–(c) shows the electrical frequency response at $_ { 1 \mathrm { - g } }$ input acceleration for type I and II. We can see that the first resonance frequency of the two devices from the measurement results is 1357.5 and $1 2 8 4 \ \mathrm { \textrm { H z } }$ , which show resemblances with the simulation results. The slight deviation mainly comes from the difference of the material properties and the damping coefficients. The maximum charges measured at the first resonance frequency are 1.59 and $3 . 1 7 \mathrm { n C }$ . When the optimal load resistances of 50 and $9 5 \ \mathrm { k } \Omega$ are coupled with piezoelectric materials of type I and II, the rms voltages 0.292 and $1 . 0 1 \mathrm { ~ V ~ }$ are measured, the generated powers of 1.705 and $1 0 . 7 3 8 ~ \mu \mathrm { W }$ are delivered. Fig. 6(d) displays the measurement of acceleration versus output power. The type I and $\mathrm { I I }$ devices are set at a range of input acceleration of $_ { \mathrm { ~ 0 . 2 - 1 ~ g ~ } }$ and the output power increases dramatically which is fitted with a nonlinear curve. To evaluate the performance of the harvester based on $\mathrm { S c } _ { 0 . 2 } \mathrm { A l } _ { 0 . 8 } \mathrm { N } / \mathrm { A l N }$ composite thin film and pure AlN. Type III and IV devices are designed to be of the same dimension but with different piezoelectric materials. A higher output charge, $1 6 . 3 \mathrm { n C }$ , generated by the type IV (ScAlN/AlN) device is related to higher piezoelectric constants compared to the type III (AlN) device, with an output charge of $1 5 . 9 6 \mathrm { \ n C }$ [Fig. 7(a)]. As shown in Fig. 7(b), the type III device generates a maximum power of $3 8 . 0 9 ~ \mu \mathrm { W }$ with a load resistance of $1 0 5 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ at a vibration frequency of $3 3 1 . 2 5 \mathrm { H z }$ . The type IV device generates the maximum power of $7 2 . 4 7 \ : \mu \mathrm { W }$ with a load resistance of $8 0 { \textrm { k } } \Omega$ at a vibration frequency of $3 3 0 . 2 5 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ . Therefore, the power generation with the introduced ScAlN film increases by $9 0 . 2 6 \%$ . In general, a typical diode bridge rectifier is used to achieve the ac–dc conversion. The higher rms voltage of composite film-based harvester is favorable for power processing circuits. The rectifier circuits consume a certain amount of electrical energy, and the output power of type III and IV devices is reduced by $3 7 . 5 9 \%$ and $3 2 . 6 7 \%$ respectively [Fig. 7(c)]. It is worth noting that the output power of the type IV device is lower than the type III device when with a low-level acceleration [Fig. 7(d)]. This is because the decrease in acceleration will cause the resonance frequency shift, making the device operate outside its resonance frequency, which demonstrates that the type IV device is more sensitive to acceleration. In this work, we simplify the $Q$ -factor contributed by the $Q \mathrm { { s } }$ and $Q _ { \mathrm { m } }$ , as follows: $$ \frac { 1 } { Q _ { \mathrm { t o t a l } } } = \frac { 1 } { Q _ { \mathrm { s } } } + \frac { 1 } { Q _ { \mathrm { m } } } . $$ The structural loss, $Q _ { \mathrm { s } }$ , is mainly determined by air damping and viscous damping. The material loss, $Q _ { \mathrm { m } }$ , is related to crystal defects and dielectric loss. Due to the influence of different beam shapes, $Q$ -factor between the trapezoid and TWC structure is different. Although the reduced surface area of the TWC structure will reduce the air damping, the reduction in bending stiffness makes the TWC softer, resulting in a small $Q \mathrm { { s } }$ . The larger harvesters having a lower $Q$ -factor compared with the smaller harvesters is mainly caused by the increasing air damping and viscous damping. The lower resonance frequency and improving electrical performance make it more suitable for environmental energy harvesting $( < 1 ~ \mathrm { \ k H z } )$ . Besides, the introduction of Sc increases the mechanic-electronic power conversion, but the $Q$ -factor decreases due to the increasing dielectric loss. The ScAlN/AlN-based energy harvester shows a wider bandwidth $( - 3 \ \mathrm { d B } )$ of $3 . 2 \ \mathrm { H z }$ than the AlN-based devices with $2 . 1 { \cdot } \mathrm { H z }$ bandwidth. The composite film improves the bandwidth and output power of the harvester at the same time. For some broadband applications, the ScAlN/AlN device has the potential to solve the problem of a significant drop in output power when the input frequency deviates from the resonance frequency. In fact, except for the ScAlN, other materials with high permittivity like PZT can also be compensated by material with low permittivities, such as PZT/AlN composite film. A short overview of the four devices and their electric characteristics is given in Table II. To enable a comparison of the generated output power to other cantilever-based designs with similar device thickness and resonance frequency, the measurements reported by Marzencki et al. [23] are added. Although the power density of the trapezoidal energy harvester in this work is lower than that of the rectangular design, a higher output power density is achieved with the TWC design (subtracting the power increase brought by the composite film), which proves the superiority of the TWC design. In addition, Mayrhofer et al. [3] evaluated the performance of energy harvesters with AlN and $\mathrm { S c } _ { 0 . 2 7 } \mathrm { A l } _ { 0 . 7 3 } \mathrm { N }$ thin films. The results showed that the power output of $\mathrm { S c } _ { 0 . 2 7 } \mathrm { A l } _ { 0 . 7 3 } \mathrm { N }$ devices $( 2 2 \ \mathrm { n W } { \cdot } \mathrm { g } ^ { - 2 } )$ increases about $50 \%$ on average compared with those fabricated with pure AlN $( 1 5 \mathrm { \ n W { \cdot g } ^ { - 2 } } )$ . Considering the $\mathrm { S c } _ { 0 . 2 } \mathrm { A l } _ { 0 . 8 } \mathrm { N } / \mathrm { A l N }$ harvester (increasing by $9 0 . 2 6 \%$ in this work, the pure ScAlN devices may not be the best choice. Further, the results in this work are in agreement with that reported by Takei et al. [24]. They designed ScAlN/AlN (2.0 $\mu \mathrm { m } / 0 . 7 ~ \mu \mathrm { m } )$ composite film device and found the generated power $( 0 . 2 1 ~ \mu \mathrm { W } )$ increases by $66 \%$ compared with the ScAlN device [24]. Based on the results of the above work, whether there is an optimal thickness ratio still needs further research.

sections.heading: V. CONCLUSION
sections.text: In summary, TWC shaped ScAlN/AlN energy harvesters ended with a proof mass are designed, fabricated, and experimentally characterized in this study. The simulated results reveal that the strain of the TWC type is significantly higher than the trapezoidal type. The proposed model of ScAlN/AlN TWC type performs high output power and ac–dc conversion efficiency compared with the traditional AlN-based trapezoidal harvester. The optimal design has a low resonance frequency of $3 3 0 . 2 5 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ , a high output power of $7 2 . 4 7 \mu \mathrm { W }$ and power density of $2 . 0 5 4 \ : \mathrm { \ m W } { \cdot } \mathrm { g } ^ { - 2 } { \cdot } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 3 }$ , which means ScAlN/AlN and corners can help optimize the mechanical and electrical response of harvesters. Piezoelectric energy harvester using ScAlN/AlN with TWC cantilever proposed in this work is a promising way to enhance the power generation and can be easily fabricated for further applications.
